title: Bees on the Rooftop
context:
A. Rooftop hives have multiplied in many cities over the past two decades. In London, the number of registered colonies rose from fewer than 1,000 in 2008 to well over 5,000 ten years later, and comparable increases have been recorded in Paris, New York and Tokyo. Enthusiasts often argue that a city is a kinder home for bees than farmland, partly because gardens and parks flower over a long season and partly because far fewer agricultural pesticides are sprayed there. Yet a growing number of ecologists are asking whether this boom is as harmless as it looks.

B. A study carried out in a group of public parks found that wherever honeybee numbers were highest, wild bumblebees and solitary bees made noticeably fewer visits to flowers. Honeybees can strip a blossom of nectar very quickly, leaving little for other insects, and many native species forage only a few hundred metres from their nests, so they cannot simply move elsewhere. The researchers pointed out that the supply of flowers in any city is finite. Adding hives without adding plants, they warned, may merely shift food from one group of pollinators to another.

C. Urban honey has become a subject of scientific curiosity as well as a popular gift. Laboratory tests on samples from several cities have detected traces of lead and cadmium, but always at levels well below the limits set for food safety. Pollen grains in a jar can also be counted under a microscope, which reveals which plants the bees visited and therefore something of the neighbourhood's vegetation. Keepers report that honey from one district can taste markedly different from honey produced only two kilometres away, a variation that supermarket blends deliberately avoid.

D. Many newcomers to the hobby lose their first colony within a year, and the cause is rarely the cold. More often the bees starve in late winter after the keeper has taken too much honey, or they are weakened by parasitic mites that went unnoticed. Beekeeping associations therefore run courses for beginners and pair them with experienced mentors who visit the hives in person. In some countries, owners are legally required to register their colonies, which allows inspectors to trace outbreaks of disease quickly and advise nearby keepers.

E. Relations with neighbours can be delicate. Surveys show that many people fear being stung, and the sight of a swarm hanging from a tree can cause alarm even though swarming bees are usually docile. Some keepers therefore place a tall fence or hedge in front of the hive entrance, forcing the bees to climb steeply and fly above head height, away from pedestrians. A number of local councils have gone further and limit how many hives a single property may hold, depending on its size. Open communication, many keepers say, prevents most disputes.

F. Conservation groups increasingly suggest that people who want to help pollinators should look beyond the honeybee. They recommend sowing wildflower strips, leaving corners of gardens untidy, and installing small wooden boxes with drilled tubes where solitary bees can nest. Some critics also doubt the motives behind hives installed on the roofs of banks and hotels, arguing that these are mainly a form of advertising which says little about genuine environmental commitment. A few companies have responded by spending their budgets on planting schemes instead of on insects.
